Stubble
STUB-ul
noun
From the Latin stipula, “a stalk,” the short, dry stalks of grain left standing in the field after the harvest is reaped.

📖 Biblical Definition

Stubble is the dry, worthless residue of the harvest — the short stalks left in the field when the grain is gathered, fit for nothing but to be burned or driven before the wind. In Scripture it is the steady image of the wicked and their works under the judgment of God. Job declares of the ungodly, “They are as stubble before the wind, and as chaff that the storm carrieth away” (Job 21:18), for the prosperity of the wicked is light and rootless, swept off in a moment. The prophet Malachi sets the same image at the last day: “Behold, the day cometh, that shall burn as an oven; and all the proud, yea, and all that do wickedly, shall be stubble: and the day that cometh shall burn them up” (Mal 4:1). Paul takes up the figure for the works of professing men: the wood, hay, and stubble built upon the foundation shall be tried by fire and consumed, though the builder himself, if he be in Christ, is saved (1Co 3:12–15). Yet stubble was not in itself contemptible, for Israel in Egypt was made to gather stubble for straw to make their bricks (Exo 5:12). The word teaches that whatever is dry, rootless, and apart from God’s life cannot stand the fire of His judgment, but is driven away and burned up in the day of the LORD.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The dry stalks left after harvest; in Scripture the image of the wicked and their works, driven before the wind and burned in judgment.

expand to see more

STUBBLE, the stalk of grain left in the field after reaping.

It is light and rootless, easily driven before the wind (Job 21:18).

It pictures the wicked, who are burned up in the day of the LORD (Mal 4:1).

Paul makes it a figure of worthless works tried by fire (1Co 3:12).

Israel gathered stubble for straw in their Egyptian bondage (Exo 5:12).

📖 Key Scripture

Job 21:18 — "They are as stubble before the wind, and as chaff that the storm carrieth away."

Mal 4:1 — "For, behold, the day cometh, that shall burn as an oven; and all the proud, yea, and all that do wickedly, shall be stubble: and the day that cometh shall burn them up, saith the LORD of hosts, that it shall leave them neither root nor branch."

1Co 3:12 — "Now if any man build upon this foundation gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, stubble;"

Exo 5:12 — "So the people were scattered abroad throughout all the land of Egypt to gather stubble instead of straw."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

An agrarian image of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; it witnesses that the wicked and their rootless works are burned up in the judgment of God.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the certainty of judgment upon all that is rootless and ungodly. Stubble is the dry remnant of the harvest, fit only for the fire; and so the LORD by it teaches that the prosperity of the wicked is light and momentary, swept off like chaff before the storm. The day cometh that shall burn as an oven, and all that do wickedly shall be stubble before it. Whatever is not rooted in the life of God cannot endure His holy fire.

The figure also searches the works of professing men, for Paul warns that wood, hay, and stubble built upon the true foundation shall be burned in the day of trial, though the builder himself, if he be in Christ, is saved yet so as by fire. The lesson is that men must build with gold and silver and precious stones — that is, with the enduring work of faith — and not with the dry stubble of self-will and vanity that the fire of God will consume.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

From the Latin stipula, a stalk; the dry residue of the reaped field, image of the wicked under judgment.
